entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen16383" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">The Overthrow of the Kingdom of the Ten Tribes - Amos 5 and <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.14">Amo 6:1-14</reference></title> <div sID="gen16384" type="x-p"/> The elegy, which the prophet commences in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.2">Amo 5:2</reference>, upon the fall of the daughter of Israel, forms the theme of the admonitory addresses in these two chapters. In every one of these sections, therefore, the proclamation of the judgment returns again, and that in a form of greater and greater intensity, till it reaches to the banishment of the whole nation, and the overthrow of Samaria and the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.27">Amo 5:27</reference>; Amo 6:8.). <div eID="gen16384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16385" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.1-Amos.5.3">Amo 5:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen16385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16386" type="x-p"/> The Elegy. - Amo 5:1. <hi type="italic">“Hear ye this word, which I raise over you; a lamentation, O house of Israel.</hi> Amo 5:2. <hi type="italic">The virgin Israel is fallen; she does not rise up again; cast down upon her soil; no one sets her up.</hi> Amo 5:3. <hi type="italic">For thus saith the Lord Jehovah, The city that goes out by a thousand will retain a hundred, and that which goes out by a hundred will retain ten, for the house of Israel.” </hi>הדּבר הזּה is still further defined in the relative clause אשׁר וגו as קינה, a mournful song, lit., a lamentation or dirge for one who is dead (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.17">2Sa 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2Ch 35:25</reference>). אשׁר is a relative pronoun, not a conjunction (for); and <hi type="italic">qı̄nâh</hi> is an explanatory apposition: which I raise or commence as (or “namely”) a lamentation. “House of Israel” is synonymous with “house of Joseph” (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Amo 5:6</reference>), hence Israel of the ten tribes. The lamentation follows in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.2">Amo 5:2</reference>, showing itself to be a song by the rhythm and by its poetical form. נפל, to fall, denotes a violent death (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">2Sa 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.25">2Sa 1:25</reference>), and is here a figure used to denote the overthrow or destruction of the kingdom. The expression virgin Israel (an epexegetical genitive, not “of Israel”) rests upon a poetical personification of the population of a city or of a kingdom, as a daughter, and wherever the further idea of being unconquered is added, as a virgin (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Isa 23:12</reference>). Here, too, the term “virgin” is used to indicate the contrast between the overthrow predicted and the original destination of Israel, as the people of God, to be unconquered by any heathen nation whatever. The second clause of the verse strengthens the first. נטּשׁ, to be stretched out or cast down, describes the fall as a violent overthrow. The third verse does not form part of the lamentation, but gives a brief, cursory vindication of it by the announcement that Israel will perish in war, even to a very small remnant. יצא refers to their marching out to war, and אלף, מאה is subordinated to it, as a more precise definition of the manner in which they marched out (cf. Ewald, §279, <hi type="italic">b</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4-Amos.5.9">Amo 5:4-9</reference> <div eID="gen16386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16387" type="x-p"/> The short, cursory explanation of the reason for the lamentation opened here, is followed in Amo 5:4. by the more elaborate proof, that Israel has deserved to be destroyed, because it has done the very opposite of what God demands of His people. God requires that they should seek Him, and forsake idolatry, in order to live (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.4-Amos.5.6">Amo 5:4-6</reference>); but Israel on the contrary, turns right into unrighteousness, without fearing the almighty God and His judgment (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.7-Amos.5.9">Amo 5:7-9</reference>). This unrighteousness God must punish (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.10-Amos.5.12">Amo 5:10-12</reference>). Amo 5:4. <hi type="italic">“For thus saith Jehovah to the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and live.</hi> Amo 5:5. <hi type="italic">And seek not Bethel, and come not to Gilgal, and go not over to Beersheba: for Gilgal repays it with captivity, and Bethel comes to nought.</hi> Amo 5:6. <hi type="italic">Seek Jehovah, and live; that He fall not upon the house of Joseph like fire, and it devour, and there be none to quench it for Bethel.” </hi> The <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">Amo 5:4</reference> is co-ordinate to that in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.3">Amo 5:3</reference>, “Seek me, and live,” for “Seek me, so shall ye live.” For this meaning of two imperatives, following directly the one upon the other, see Gesenius, §130, 2, and Ewald, §347, <hi type="italic">b.</hi> חיה, not merely to remain alive, not to perish, but to obtain possession of true life. God can only be sought, however, in His revelation, or in the manner in which He wishes to be sought and worshipped. This explains the antithesis, “Seek not Bethel,” etc. In addition to Bethel and Gilgal (see at <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4">Amo 4:4</reference>), Beersheba, which was in the southern part of Judah, is also mentioned here, being the place where Abraham had called upon the Lord (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.33">Gen 21:33</reference>), and where the Lord had appeared to Isaac and Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.24">Gen 26:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1">Gen 46:1</reference>; see also at <reference osisRef="Gen.21.31">Gen 21:31</reference>). These sacred reminiscences from the olden time had caused Beersheba to be made into a place of idolatrous worship, to which the Israelites went on pilgrimage beyond the border of their own kingdom (עבר). But visiting these idolatrous places of worship did no good, for the places themselves would be given up to destruction. Gilgal would wander into <hi type="italic">captivity</hi> (an expression used here on account of the similarity in the ring of גּלגּל and גּלה יגלה). Bethel would become <hi type="italic">'âven</hi>, that is to say, not “an idol” here, but “nothingness,” though there is an allusion to the change of <hi type="italic">Beth - el</hi> (God’s house) into <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>-<hi type="italic">'âven</hi> (an idol-house; see at Hos 4:15). The Judaean Beersheba is passed over in the threat, because the primary intention of Amos is simply to predict the destruction of the kingdom of the ten tribes. After this warning the prophet repeats the exhortation to seek Jehovah, and adds this threatening, “that Jehovah come not like fire upon the house of Joseph” (<hi type="italic">tsâlach</hi>, generally construed with <hi type="italic">‛al</hi> or <hi type="italic">'el</hi>, cf. Jdg 14:19; Jdg 15:14; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.6">1Sa 10:6</reference>; here with an accusative, to fall upon a person), “and it (the fire) devour, without there being any to extinguish it for Bethel.” Bethel, as the chief place of worship in Israel, is mentioned here for the kingdom itself, which is called the “house of Joseph,” from Joseph the father of Ephraim, the most powerful tribe in that kingdom. <div eID="gen16387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16388" type="x-p"/> To add force to this warning, Amos (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.7-Amos.5.9">Amo 5:7-9</reference>) exhibits the moral corruption of the Israelites, in contrast with the omnipotence of Jehovah as it manifests itself in terrible judgments. Amo 5:7. <hi type="italic">“They that change right into wormwood, and bring righteousness down to the earth.</hi> Amo 5:8. <hi type="italic">He that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into morning, and darkeneth day to night: that calleth to the waters of the sea, and poureth them over the surface of the earth; Jehovah is His name.</hi> Amo 5:9. <hi type="italic">Who causeth desolation to flash upon the strong, and desolation cometh upon the fortress.” </hi> The sentences in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Amo 5:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">Amo 5:8</reference> are written without any connecting link. The participle in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Amo 5:7</reference> cannot be taken as an address, for it is carried on in the third person (<hi type="italic">hinnı̄chū</hi>), not in the second. And <hi type="italic">hahōphekhı̄m</hi> (who turn) cannot be in apposition to <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>-<hi type="italic">el</hi>, since the latter refers not to the inhabitants, but to the houses. As Amos is generally fond of a participial construction (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">Amo 4:13</reference>), so in a spirited address he likes to utter the thoughts one after another without any logical link of connection. As a matter of fact, <hi type="italic">hahōphekhı̄m</hi> is connected with <hi type="italic">bēth</hi>-<hi type="italic">yōsēph</hi> (the house of Joseph), “Seek the Lord, ye of the house of Joseph, who turn right into wrong;” but instead of this connection, he proceeds with a simple description, They are turning,” etc. <hi type="italic">La‛ănâh</hi>, wormwood, a bitter plant, is a figurative term denoting bitter wrong (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.6.12">Amo 6:12</reference>), the actions of men being regarded, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.29.17">Deu 29:17</reference>, as the fruits of their state of mind. Laying righteousness on the ground (<hi type="italic">hinnı̄ăch</hi> from <hi type="italic">nūăch</hi>) answers to our “trampling under feet.” Hitzig has correctly explained the train of thought in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Amo 5:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.8">Amo 5:8</reference> : “They do this, whereas Jehovah is the Almighty, and can bring destruction suddenly upon them.” To show this antithesis, the article which takes the place of the relative is omitted from the participles <hi type="italic">‛ōsēh</hi> and <hi type="italic">hōphēkh</hi>. The description of the divine omnipotence commences with the creation of the brightly shining stars; then follow manifestations of this omnipotence, which are repeated in the government of the world. <hi type="italic">Kı̄mâh</hi>, lit., the crowd, is the group of seven stars, the constellation of the Pleiades. <hi type="italic">Kesı̄l</hi>, the gate, according to the ancient versions the giant, is the constellation of Orion. The two are mentioned together in <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference> (see Delitzsch on the latter). And He also turns the darkest night into morning, and darkens the day into night again. These words refer to the regular interchange of day and night; for <hi type="italic">tsalmâveth</hi>, the shadow of death, i.e., thick darkness, never denotes the regularly recurring gloominess of night, but the appalling gloom of night (<reference osisRef="Job.24.17">Job 24:17</reference>), more especially of the night of death (<reference osisRef="Job.3.5">Job 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.21-Job.10.22">Job 10:21-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.17">Job 38:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.20">Psa 44:20</reference>), the unlighted depth of the heart of the earth (<reference osisRef="Job.28.3">Job 28:3</reference>), the darkness of the prison (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.10">Psa 107:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.14">Psa 107:14</reference>), also of wickedness (<reference osisRef="Job.12.22">Job 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.22">Job 34:22</reference>), of sufferings (<reference osisRef="Job.16.16">Job 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jer 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>), and of spiritual misery (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference>). Consequently the words point to the judicial rule of the Almighty in the world. As the Almighty turns the darkness of death into light, and the deepest misery into prosperity and health,<note placement="foot">Theodoret has given a correct explanation, though he does not quite exhaust the force of the words: “It is easy for Him to turn even the greatest dangers into happiness; for by the shadow of death he means great dangers. And it is also easy to bring calamity upon those who are in prosperity.”</note> so He darkens the bright day of prosperity into the dark night of adversity, and calls to the waters of the sea to pour themselves over the earth like the flood, and to destroy the ungodly. The idea that by the waters of the sea, which pour themselves out at the call of God over the surface of the earth, we are to understand the moisture which rises from the sea and then falls upon the earth as rain, no more answers to the words themselves, than the idea expressed by Hitzig, that they refer to the water of the rivers and brooks, which flow out of the sea as well as into it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Ecc 1:7</reference>). The words suggest the thought of terrible inundations of the earth by the swelling of the sea, and the allusion to the judgment of the flood can hardly be overlooked. This judicial act of the Almighty, no strong man and no fortress can defy. With the swiftness of lightning He causes desolation to smite the strong man. <hi type="italic">Bâlag</hi>, lit., <hi type="italic">micare</hi>, used in the Arabic to denote the lighting up of the rays of the dawn, <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> to cause to light up, is applied here to motion with the swiftness of lightning; it is also employed in a purely metaphorical sense for the lighting up of the countenance (Ps. 39:14; <reference osisRef="Job.9.27">Job 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.20">Job 10:20</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.5.9">Amo 5:9</reference></hi> the address is continued in a descriptive form; יבוא has not a causative meaning. The two clauses of this verse point to the fate which awaits the Israelites who trust in their strength and their fortifications (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.13">Amo 6:13</reference>). And yet they persist in unrighteousness.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10-Amos.5.12">Amo 5:10-12</reference> <hi type="italic">“They hate the monitor in the gate, and abhor him that speaketh uprightly. </hi> Amo 5:11. <hi type="italic">Therefore, because ye tread upon the poor, and take the distribution of corn from him, ye have built houses of square stones, and will not dwell therein; planted pleasant vineyards, and will not drink their wine.</hi> Amo 5:12. <hi type="italic">For I know how many are your transgressions, and how great your sins; oppressing the righteous, taking atonement money; and ye bow down the poor in the gate.” </hi> However natural it may seem to take מוכיח and דּבר תּמים in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10">Amo 5:10</reference> as referring to prophets, who charge the ungodly with their acts of unrighteousness, as Jerome does, this explanation is precluded not only by <hi type="italic">bassha‛ar</hi> (in the gate), since the gate was not the meeting-place of the people where the prophets were accustomed to stand, but the place where courts of judgment were held, and all the public affairs of the community discussed (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.21.19">Deu 21:19</reference>); but also by the first half of <reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>, which presupposes judicial proceedings. <hi type="italic">Mōkhı̄ăch</hi> is not merely the judge who puts down unjust accusers, but any one who lifts up his voice in a court of justice against acts of injustice (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa 29:21</reference>). דּבר תּמים, he who says what is blameless, i.e., what is right and true: this is to be taken generally, and not to be restricted to the accused who seeks to defend his innocence. תּעב is a stronger expression than שׂנא. The punishment for this unjust oppression of the poor will be the withdrawal of their possessions. The ἁπ. λεγ. <hi type="italic">bōshēs</hi> is a dialectically different form for בוסס, from בוּס, to trample down (Rashi, Kimchi), analogous to the interchange of שׁריון and סריון, a coat of mail, although as a rule שׁ passes into ס, and not ס into שׁ. For the derivation from בושׁ, according to which בושׁס would stand for בושׁשׁ (Hitzig and Tuch on Genesis p. 85), is opposed both to the construction with על, and also to the circumstance that בּושׁשׁ means to delay (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">Exo 32:1</reference>; Jdg 5:28); and the derivation suggested by Hitzig from an Arabic verb, signifying to carry one’s self haughtily towards others, is a mere loophole. Taking a gift of corn from the poor refers to unjust extortion on the part of the judge, who will only do justice to a poor man when he is paid for it. The main clause, which was introduced with <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi>, is continued with בּתּי גזית: “thus have ye built houses of square stones, and shall not dwell therein;” for “ye shall not dwell in the houses of square stones which ye have built.” The threat is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deu 28:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.39">Deu 28:39</reference>, and sets before them the plundering of the land and the banishment of the people. Houses built of square stones are splendid buildings (see <reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">Isa 9:9</reference>). The reason for this threat is given in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.12">Amo 5:12</reference>, where reference is made to the multitude and magnitude of the sins, of which injustice in the administration of justice is again held up as the chief sin. The participles צררי and לקחי are attached to the suffixes of פּשׁעיכם and חטּאתיכם: <hi type="italic">your</hi> sins, who oppress the righteous, attack him, and take atonement money, contrary to the express command of the law in Num 35:31, to take no <hi type="italic">kōpher</hi> for the soul of a murderer. The judges allowed the rich murderer to purchase exemption from capital punishment by the payment of atonement money, whilst they bowed down the right of the poor. Observe the transition from the participle to the third person fem., by which the prophet turns away with disgust from these ungodly judges. Bowing down the poor is a concise expression for bowing down the right of the poor: compare <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference> and the warnings against this sin (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.6">Exo 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">Deu 16:19</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference> <div eID="gen16388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16389" type="x-p"/> With the new turn that all talking is useless, Amos repeats the admonition to seek good and hate evil, if they would live and obtain favour with God  (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.13-Amos.5.15">Amo 5:13-15</reference>); and then appends the threat that deep mourning will arise on every hand, since God is drawing near to judgment. Amo 5:13. <hi type="italic">“Therefore, whoever has prudence at this time is silent, for it is an evil time.” </hi> As <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) always introduces the threatening of divine punishment after the exposure of the sins (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Amo 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Amo 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.11">Amo 3:11</reference>), we might be disposed to connect <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference> with the preceding verse; but the contents of the verse require that it should be taken in connection with what follows, so that <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> simply denote the close connection of the two turns of speech, i.e., indicates that the new command in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Amo 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.15">Amo 5:15</reference> is a consequence of the previous warnings. <hi type="italic">Hammaskı̄l</hi>, the prudent man, he who acts wisely, is silent. בּעת ההיא, at a time such as this is, because it is an evil time, not however “a dangerous time to speak, on account of the malignity of those in power,” but a time of moral corruption, in which all speaking and warning are of no avail. It is opposed to the context to refer בעת ההיא to the future, i.e., to the time when God will come to punish, in which case the silence would be equivalent to not murmuring against God (Rashi and others). At the same time, love to his people, and zeal for their deliverance, impel the prophet to repeat his call to them to return.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14-Amos.5.15">Amo 5:14-15</reference> <hi type="italic">“Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live; and so Jehovah the God of hosts may be with you, as ye say.</hi> Amo 5:15. <hi type="italic">Hate evil, and love good, and set up justice in the gate; perhaps Jehovah the God of hosts will show favour to the remnant of Joseph.” </hi> The command to seek and love good is practically the same as that to seek the Lord in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.4">Amo 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Amo 5:6</reference>; and therefore the promise is the same, “that ye may live.” But it is only in fellowship with God that man has life. This truth the Israelites laid hold of in a perfectly outward sense, fancying that they stood in fellowship with God by virtue of their outward connection with the covenant nation as sons of Israel or Abraham (cf. Joh 8:39), and that the threatened judgment could not reach them, but that God would deliver them in every time of oppression by the heathen (cf. Mic 3:11; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">Jer 7:10</reference>). Amos meets this delusion with the remark, “that Jehovah may be so with you as ye say.” כּן neither means “in case ye do so” (Rashi, Baur), nor “in like manner as, i.e., if ye strive after good” (Hitzig). Neither of these meanings can be established, and here they are untenable, for the simple reason that כּן unmistakeably corresponds with the following כּאשׁר. It means nothing more than “so as ye say.” The thought is the following: “Seek good, and not evil: then will Jehovah the God of the heavenly hosts be with you as a helper in distress, so as ye say.” This implied that in their present condition, so long as they sought good, they ought not to comfort themselves with the certainty of Jehovah’s help. Seeking good is explained in v. 15 as loving good, and this is still further defined as setting up justice in the gate, i.e., maintaining a righteous administration of justice at the place of judgment; and to this the hope, so humiliating to carnal security, is attached: perhaps God will then show favour to the remnant of the people. The emphasis in these words is laid as much upon <hi type="italic">perhaps</hi> as upon the remnant of Joseph. Amo 5:16. <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith Jehovah the God of hosts, the Lord: In all roads lamentation! and in all streets will men say, Alas! alas! and they call the husbandman to mourning, and lamentation to those skilled in lamenting.</hi> Amo 5:17. <hi type="italic">And in all vineyards lamentation, because I go through the midst of thee, saith Jehovah.” Lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) is not connected with the admonitions in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Amo 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.15">Amo 5:15</reference>, nor can it point back to the reproaches in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.7">Amo 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10-Amos.5.12">Amo 5:10-12</reference>, since they are too far off: it rather links on to the substance of <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference>, which involves the thought that all admonition to return is fruitless, and the ungodly still persist in their unrighteousness, - a thought which also forms the background of <reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Amo 5:14</reference>, Amo 5:15. The meaning of <reference osisRef="Amos.5.16">Amo 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.17">Amo 5:17</reference> is, that mourning and lamentation for the dead will fill both city and land. On every hand will there be dead to weep for, because Jehovah will go judging through the land. The roads and streets are not merely those of the capital, although these are primarily to be thought of, but those of all the towns in the kingdom. <hi type="italic">Mispēd</hi> is the death-wail. This is evident from the parallel <hi type="italic">'âmar hō hō</hi>, saying, Alas, alas! i.e., striking up the death-wail (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jer 22:18</reference>). And this death-wail will not be heard in all the streets of the towns only, but the husbandman will also be called from the field to mourn, i.e., to seep for one who has died in his house. The verb קראוּ, they call, belongs to מספּד אל י, they call lamentation to those skilled in mourning: for they call out the word <hi type="italic">mispēd</hi> to the professional mourners; in other words, they send for them to strike up their wailing for the dead. ידעי נהי (those skilled in mourning) are the public wailing women, who were hired when a death occurred to sing mourning songs (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.9.16">Jer 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.23">Mat 9:23</reference>, and my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäologie</hi>, ii. p. 105). Even in all the vineyards, the places where rejoicing is generally looked for (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.11">Amo 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">Isa 16:10</reference>), the death-wail will be heard. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.5.17">Amo 5:17</reference></hi> mentions the event which occasions the lamentation everywhere. כּי, for (not “if”) I go through the midst of thee. These words are easily explained from <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exo 12:12</reference>, from which Amos has taken them. Jehovah there says to Moses, “I pass through the land of Egypt, and smite all the first-born.” And just as the Lord once passed through Egypt, so will He now pass judicially through Israel, and slay the ungodly. For Israel is no longer the nation of the covenant, which He passes over and spares (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">Amo 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Amo 8:2</reference>), but has become an Egypt, which He will pass through as a judge to punish it. This threat is carried out still further in the next two sections, commencing with <hi type="italic">hōi</hi>.

What good is the day of Jehovah to you? It is darkness, and not light.</hi> Amo 5:19. <hi type="italic">As if a man fleeth before the lion, and the bear meets him; and he comes into the house, and rests his hand upon the wall, and the snake bites him.</hi> Amo 5:20. <hi type="italic">Alas! is not the day of Jehovah darkness, and not light; and gloom, and no brightness in it?” </hi> As the Israelites rested their hope of deliverance from every kind of hostile oppression upon their outward connection with the covenant nation (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Amo 5:14</reference>); many wished the day to come, on which Jehovah would judge all the heathen, and redeem Israel out of all distress, and exalt it to might and dominion above all nations, and bless it with honour and glory, applying the prophecy of Joel in ch. 3 without the least reserve to Israel as the nation of Jehovah, and without considering that, according to <reference osisRef="Joel.2.32">Joe 2:32</reference>, those only would be saved on the day of Jehovah who called upon the name of the Lord, and were called by the Lord, i.e., were acknowledged by the Lord as His own. These infatuated hopes, which confirmed the nation in the security of its life of sin, are met by Amos with an exclamation of woe upon those who long for the day of Jehovah to come, and with the declaration explanatory of the woe, that that day is darkness and not light, and will bring them nothing but harm and destruction, and not prosperity and salvation. He explains this in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Amo 5:19</reference> by a figure taken from life. To those who wish the day of Jehovah to come, the same thing will happen as to a man who, when fleeing from a lion, meets a bear, etc. The meaning is perfectly clear: whoever would escape one danger, falls into a second; and whoever escapes this, falls into a third, and perishes therein. The serpent’s bite in the hand is fatal. “In that day every place is full of danger and death; neither in-doors nor out-of-doors is any one safe: for out-of-doors lions and bears prowl about, and in-doors snakes lie hidden, even in the holes of the walls” (C. a. Lap.). After this figurative indication of the sufferings and calamities which the day of the Lord will bring, Amos once more repeats in v. 20, in a still more emphatic manner (הלא, <hi type="italic">nonne</hi> = assuredly), that it will be no day of salvation, sc. to those who seek evil and not good, and trample justice and righteousness under foot (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.14">Amo 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.15">Amo 5:15</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21-Amos.5.24">Amo 5:21-24</reference> <div eID="gen16391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16392" type="x-p"/> This threatening judgment will not be averted by the Israelites, even by their feasts and sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Amo 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Amo 5:22</reference>). The Lord has no pleasure in the feasts which they celebrate. Their outward, heartless worship, does not make them into the people of God, who can count upon His grace. Amo 5:21. <hi type="italic">“I hate, I despise your feasts, and do not like to smell your holy days.</hi> Amo 5:22. <hi type="italic">For if ye offer me burnt-offerings, and your meat-offerings, I have no pleasure therein; and the thank-offering of your fatted calves I do not regard.</hi> Amo 5:23. <hi type="italic">Put away from me the noise of thy songs; and I do not like to hear the playing of thy harps.</hi> Amo 5:24. <hi type="italic">And let judgment roll like water, and righteousness like an inexhaustible stream.” </hi> By the rejection of the <hi type="italic">opus operatum</hi> of the feasts and sacrifices, the roots are cut away from the false reliance of the Israelites upon their connection with the people of God. The combination of the words שׂנאתי מאסתּי expresses in the strongest terms the dislike of God to the feasts of those who were at enmity with Him. <hi type="italic">Chaggı̄m</hi> are the great annual feasts; <hi type="italic">‛ătsârōth</hi>, the meetings for worship at those feasts, inasmuch as a holy meeting took place at the <hi type="italic">‛ătsereth</hi> of the feast of Passover and feast of Tabernacles (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev 23:36</reference>). <hi type="italic">Rı̄ăch</hi>, to smell, is an expression of satisfaction, with an allusion to the ריח ניחוח, which ascended to God from the burning sacrifice (see <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">Lev 26:31</reference>). <hi type="italic">Kı̄</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Amo 5:22</reference>, is explanatory: “for,” not “yea.” The observance of the feast culminated in the sacrificers. God did not like the feasts, because He had no pleasure in the sacrifices. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Amo 5:23</reference></hi> the two kinds of sacrifice, <hi type="italic">‛ōlâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">minchâh</hi>, are divided between the protasis and apodosis, which gives rise to a certain incongruity. The sentences, if written fully, would read thus: When ye offer me burnt-offerings and meat-offerings, I have no pleasure in your burnt-offerings and meat-offerings. To these two kinds the <hi type="italic">shelem</hi>, the health-offering or peace-offering, is added as a third class in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.5.22">Amo 5:22</reference></hi>. מריאים, fattened things, generally mentioned along with <hi type="italic">bâqâr</hi> as one particular species, for fattened calves (see <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa 1:11</reference>).
